strengths: Clear problem framing: the paper articulates three concrete limitations (interference, redundancy, routing ambiguity) of coarse-grained MoE-LoRA designs in continual learning, and its rank-one decomposition with self-activation is a well-motivated response grounded in a linear associative-memory view of LoRA updates (Sec. 3.2), which gives the design conceptual coherence.

Broad and convincing empirical coverage: results span vision-language CL (X-TAIL Table 1, MTIL Table 11), T5-large (Table 3), 15-task long sequences (Table 8), LLaMA2-7B (Table 9), and a fine-tuning forgetting/generalization study on Llama-3.1-8B (Table 2), with consistent improvements over strong recent baselines (RAIL-Primal, CoDyRA, O-LoRA, LB-CL, InfLoRA).

Good parameter efficiency: MoRA achieves these gains with comparable or fewer trainable parameters than standard LoRA (Table 10) and lower GPU memory (Table 15), and the claim of lower activation cost is quantified (e.g., ~1/3 of activated parameters vs rank-32 LoRA).

Thorough ablations: Table 4 isolates routing/activation strategy, Fig. 4 varies activation budget, temperature, and threshold; appendix provides 3-run mean±std comparisons (Table 13), alternative task orderings (Table 14), and activation visualizations (Figs. 3, 5, 6) plus rank-sparsity statistics (Figs. 7-9) that directly probe the specialization and reuse claims.

Honest handling of some design choices, e.g., acknowledging that load-balancing losses are unnecessary for their gate, and that optimal temperature varies across architectures; LLM usage disclosure is appropriate.
weaknesses: Moderate/incremental novelty: rank-level decomposition of LoRA updates into independently gated components is closely related to existing work the paper itself cites (Mixture-of-Subspaces Wu et al. 2024a, MiLoRA, MoSLoRA, CoDyRA's per-rank weights). The main genuinely new elements — using key activations A_i x as self-routing gates, temperature sharpening, and test-time thresholding — are relatively simple heuristics rather than a substantive methodological advance.

Mixed evidence for the self-activation claim: in Table 4, self-activation alone (60.26 Transfer) underperforms the coarse MoE-LoRA baseline (62.56), and most of the gain comes from the combination of top-k masking, temperature scaling, and thresholding. The narrative that self-activation 'matches or surpasses a separately learned router' is only weakly supported and depends on cherry-picked configurations; the paper's central causal story about routing ambiguity is not isolated experimentally.

Forgetting prevention is largely architectural: prior ranks are frozen after each task, so improved 'Last' scores partially follow from the freezing strategy shared with O-LoRA/InfLoRA/CoDyRA; the paper does not disentangle the contribution of fine-grained routing from that of incremental freezing.

Unaddressed inference cost and scaling: scoring all r_t accumulated ranks per token means compute grows linearly with task count (160+ ranks after 10 tasks); no inference latency/FLOPs comparison is provided, and the practicality at very long task sequences is not demonstrated.

Hyperparameter sensitivity and reproducibility gaps: τ_MoRA, δ, and k are set per experiment (τ=0.1 for CLIP/T5 but 0.5 for Llama) with no principled selection procedure, raising tuning-burden and generalization concerns; code is only promised 'upon acceptance,' so claims cannot yet be independently verified.

Some results are modest or hard to interpret: MMLU improvements in Table 2 are within ~0.3 points of baselines on several subjects, and a few Transfer gains over CoDyRA in Table 1 are within reported standard deviations, weakening the strength of the SOTA claims in these cases.

strengths: Broad and fairly comprehensive empirical validation: the method is evaluated on CLIP-based CL (X-TAIL and MTIL, with multiple task orders), standard LM CL benchmarks with T5-large and LLaMA2-7B (Tables 3, 8, 9), and a fine-tuning forgetting/generalization study on Llama3.1-8B (Table 2), covering Transfer/Average/Last metrics consistently with prior work.

The core idea — treating each rank-one LoRA component as a fine-grained expert and reusing its key vector A_i as the relevance signal, avoiding a separate router — is clean, parameter-efficient (Table 10: rd_in + kd_out per task), and well-motivated via the linear associative-memory framing (Sec. 3.2).

Useful ablations on routing strategy, activation budget, temperature, and test-time thresholding (Table 4, Fig. 4), plus qualitative rank-activation visualizations (Figs. 3, 5, 6) and statistical analyses of sparsity across layers/modules (Figs. 7–9) that go beyond average accuracy reporting.
Variance is reported over three runs for the main comparison (Table 13), and hyperparameters, task orderings, and dataset details are documented sufficiently for reproduction attempts.
weaknesses: The central 'self-activation' narrative is only weakly supported by the paper's own ablation. In Table 4, Self-activation (60.26/65.94/69.85) is statistically indistinguishable from a trainable rank-level router, Non-self-activation (60.09/65.97/69.76), and both are substantially WORSE than coarse-grained MoE-LoRA (62.56/69.45/74.53). The claimed gains materialize mainly from the temperature-based sharpness control (71.15/79.62) and the full stack, not from the self-activation mechanism itself. This undercuts the three-challenge story (interference/redundancy/ambiguity) attributed to coarse routing.

The mechanism itself is close to standard LoRA forward computation: s_i = A_i x is exactly the score LoRA already computes densely; the novelty reduces to applying top-k masking, a temperature on the softmax, and a test-time threshold to existing activations, combined with the standard freeze-old-ranks-per-task strategy. Given closely related prior work (CoDyRA's rank-selective LoRA, MoSLoRA/mixture-of-subspaces, InfLoRA), the methodological delta over Lu et al. (2024) is essentially input-dependent (vs. fixed) rank weights plus sparsification heuristics — an incremental contribution.

No theoretical or empirical analysis of gradient flow under top-k masking during training: ranks not selected receive no gradient, which interacts nontrivially with incremental rank addition; the paper asserts this 'prevents tiny, noisy activations from affecting gradients' but provides no evidence for training dynamics or failure modes (e.g., newly initialized ranks never being selected).

Transfer gains are marginal relative to the zero-shot baseline (63.3 vs. 62.4 on X-TAIL; 69.7 vs. 69.4 on MTIL) and often below competing methods; the strong headline improvements are concentrated in Average/Last, where comparisons partly rely on numbers copied from prior papers under possibly non-identical settings rather than re-run baselines.

The 'training objectives' claim that no load-balancing is needed is asserted from observation only, and the conclusion acknowledges the temperature/threshold hyperparameters are sensitive across architectures (τ = 0.1 for CLIP/T5, τ = 0.5 for Llama3.1), suggesting tuning burden that is not characterized.
Presentation has rough edges (e.g., 'Conceptional illustration', several grammatical issues), and code is only promised upon acceptance, limiting immediate reproducibility.

strengths: Well-motivated framing: the paper clearly articulates three intertwined failure modes (interference, redundancy, routing ambiguity) of adapter-level MoE-LoRA in continual learning and connects them to a concrete design remedy — treating each rank-one component as an expert.

The self-activation mechanism (using LoRA's A matrix keys as routers for their own B values) is elegant: it removes a separate router, saves parameters, and is grounded in the linear associative-memory view of weights (Sec. 3.2). Ablation Table 4 supports that raw activation scores match or beat a trained router with 1.5x parameters.

Comprehensive empirical validation across modalities and settings: X-TAIL and MTIL with CLIP, standard and 15-task long sequences on T5-large, LLaMA2-7B CL, and a fine-tuning-only study on Llama3.1-8B (HumanEval + MMLU out-of-domain), including multi-run mean/std comparisons (Table 13) and a second X-TAIL ordering (Table 14).

Consistently strong results: state-of-the-art Average/Last on X-TAIL (72.7/80.9 vs. CoDyRA 71.3/79.2), close to MTL upper bound on T5-large (77.6 vs 80.0), and matched HumanEval Pass@1 to rank-32 LoRA with roughly one-third the activated parameters.

Thorough analysis beyond headline numbers: activation-budget, temperature, and threshold ablations (Fig. 4), per-layer/module sparsity statistics (Figs. 7–9), and visualizations demonstrating rank specialization, knowledge reuse, and forgetting mitigation (Figs. 3, 5, 6).
Honest limitations discussion in the conclusion (e.g., temperature choice is currently manual and data-distribution-unaware), and an explicit LLM-usage statement.
weaknesses: Novelty is solid but incremental: decomposing LoRA updates into rank-one mixtures with learned gates is close to existing mixture-of-subspaces work (Wu et al., 2024a MoSLoRA; LoRAMoE; MiLoRA), and key-based routing recalls memory/attention intuitions. The paper's differentiation lies mostly in the CL context, the self-activation (no external router), and the specific sparsity controls; the positioning against MoSLoRA-style methods could be sharper.

The ablation in Table 4 is confusing and weakens the evidence for individual components: it is unclear whether rows are additive configurations or independent ones — e.g., 'w/ test-time rank thresholding' (60.78/66.83/71.08) scores below 'w/ sharpness control' (62.07/71.15/79.62) yet both are presented as part of MoRA (63.30/72.70/80.90). The additive-versus-isolated structure and the claimed 'slight gain' from thresholding need clarification.

Hyperparameter sensitivity: the optimal temperature and threshold differ across models (τ=0.1 for CLIP/T5, τ=0.5 for Llama3.1; δ=0.2), and Fig. 4b shows transfer varies dramatically with τ. This reduces out-of-the-box applicability, which the authors acknowledge, but no practical selection heuristic is offered.

Some central claims are asserted more than measured: 'redundancy' and 'routing ambiguity' of MoE-LoRA are motivating problems, but the paper provides limited direct quantitative evidence of expert duplication/route drift in baselines (beyond end-task forgetting numbers). The claim that earlier-task routing degrades as experts accumulate is not directly verified.

Code is only promised 'upon acceptance' (reproducibility statement), so results cannot yet be independently verified; several important comparisons (MTIL Table 11, LLaMA2-7B Table 9, long sequences Table 8) are deferred to the appendix.

Minor: some gains over the strongest baseline (CoDyRA) are within about one standard deviation on several metrics (e.g., Transfer 63.3±0.26 vs 63.2±0.28; some Last columns), so the headline 'substantially outperforms' is more accurate for Average/Last than for Transfer.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple CL regimes: X-TAIL and MTIL for CLIP, TRACE for LLMs (LLaMA-2, Gemma, LLaMA-3-1B), standard T5-large CL benchmarks, 15-task long sequences, SuperNI, and code-generation fine-tuning, with consistent SOTA or competitive results (e.g., 72.7 Avg / 80.9 Last on X-TAIL; 44.54 OP / 1.37 BWT on TRACE LLaMA-2).

The core mechanism is simple and parameter-efficient: decomposing rank-r LoRA updates into atomic rank-1 experts with intrinsic key-based routing removes the external router (Table 11 shows r*din + k*dout trainable params, lower than MoE-LoRA variants), and Table 18 confirms a low memory footprint (4.4M trainable params, comparable to CoDyRA).

Well-designed ablation of routing strategies (Table 4) isolates the contribution of self-activation, top-k sparsity, temperature scaling, and thresholding; hyperparameter sensitivity is probed in Fig. 4.

Unusually thorough analysis sections: rank-activation visualizations (Figs. 3, 6, 7), aggregated activation heatmaps (Fig. 5), statistical sparsity analyses (Figs. 8-10), order-robustness analysis (Table 14), variance across 3 runs (Table 16), and pruning analysis (Table 19) collectively support the claimed specialization/stability behavior.

Honest treatment of caveats in places (e.g., acknowledgment that optimal temperature varies across architectures, that further regularization might help, and a substantive impact statement discussing potential misuse of lightweight updates).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The core algorithm is essentially sparse per-rank gating on LoRA factors: the self-activation score (Eq. 5) is a normalized key-input inner product, top-k selection, softmax, and thresholding are all standard MoE components, and fine-grained rank-level mixtures already exist (e.g., MoSLoRA/mixture-of-subspaces [87], MoE-LoRA fine-grained variants [15, 51]). The 'linear associative memory' framing largely reinterprets LoRA key-value structure (related also to the key-value view of transformer layers) and is asserted more than it yields new technical content.

The headline framing ('eliminates routers', 'no extra parameters') is somewhat diluted: the trained key vectors A now serve both representation and routing, so routing capacity is still being learned; and the method actually adds several new hyperparameters (k, tau_MoRAM, delta, per-model temperature tuning) whose tuning burden is not fully accounted for in comparisons.

Claims about coarse-grained MoE-LoRA failure modes (interference, redundancy, routing collapse) are motivated narratively but only indirectly verified; Table 4 shows the learned external router underperforms, but no direct measurement of routing drift/collapse is provided.

Capacity/fairness concerns in CL comparisons: MoRAM accumulates rank-1 atoms per task (r=16 per task, frozen), so total memory grows with tasks, while several baselines (e.g., fixed-rank O-LoRA, InfLoRA) maintain bounded size; comparisons at matched total parameter budgets across the full task sequence are not reported. Some baseline entries in Table 1 (RAIL-Primal transfer/average) are also ceiling-constrained, as the authors themselves note.

Ablation table presentation is confusing: in Table 4, rows appear to be cumulative, but 'MoRAM (Full)' (63.30/72.70/80.90) jumps far beyond the threshold-selection row (60.78/66.83/71.08) without an explicit accounting of which remaining factor drives this gap, weakening the component-wise attribution.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no code release is mentioned anywhere, and the method has multiple dataset-specific settings (temperature 0.5/0.1/0.03/0.03, varying r and k per benchmark) that would be hard to replicate without code.

The overall arc — 'fine-grained experts + intrinsic routing works better for CL' — is a useful but incremental refinement within an already crowded MoE-LoRA CL literature; significance for the broader ML community is moderate and specialized to PEFT-based continual learning.

strengths: The core idea—treating rank-1 LoRA components as atomic, content-addressable memory units with self-activated routing that eliminates external routers—is clean, well-motivated, and conceptually appealing.

Evaluation coverage is unusually broad: X-TAIL and MTIL on CLIP, TRACE on three LLMs, standard and 15-task language classification streams, SuperNI, and a CodeAlpaca/forgetting study, with consistent (if sometimes modest) gains.

The paper includes genuine ablations of each design component (routing strategy, activation budget, temperature, threshold), parameter-count comparisons (Tables 11, 18), rank-pruning analysis (Table 19), and qualitative plus statistical visualizations of rank specialization and reuse.

Honest and reasonably thorough limitations/impact discussion, including acknowledgment of potential misuse (backdoors, bias entrenchment) and sensitivity of the temperature hyperparameter across architectures.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work. Decomposing LoRA into rank-1 experts with input-dependent per-rank gating is essentially the design of MoLE (Mixture of LoRA Experts, Wu et al., ICLR 2024) and mixture-of-subspaces LoRA [87], both cited only briefly without head-to-head comparison. The main new element is the key-based self-activation score, which is a simple inner-product softmax; the paper's framing (associative memory, 'content-addressable retrieval') dresses up a fairly incremental mechanism in ambitious language.

The central claims about coarse-grained MoE-LoRA (interference, redundancy, routing collapse) are asserted rather than demonstrated. No experiment directly shows router collapse or expert drift in the baselines; the failure modes motivating the method remain hypothetical.

Ablation results (Table 4) are confusing and internally inconsistent: e.g., threshold-based selection yields Transfer 60.78, lower than temperature scaling (62.07), yet the full model reaches 63.30, and the rows do not compose transparently. This undermines confidence in which components actually drive the gains—temperature alone (row 5) recovers most of the improvement, suggesting the headline mechanism (self-activation vs. external router) contributes little (60.26 vs. 60.09).

Extremely low temperatures (τ = 0.01–0.05) make the softmax effectively a hard argmax, meaning the method may largely reduce to nearest-atom hard routing plus several other hand-tuned sparsity mechanisms (top-k, threshold δ). The Appendix concedes the optimal temperature differs per model, and multiple coupled hyperparameters (k, τ, δ, r) with no sensitivity analysis of their interaction raise fragility and reproducibility concerns; no code release is mentioned.

Empirical gains are often marginal despite strong claims: TRACE OP improvements are ~1% over TreeLoRA; X-TAIL Last is 80.9 vs. 79.1/79.2 for RAIL/CoDyRA; on 15-task sequences (Table 9) MoRAM (69.72) barely edges LB-CL (69.2) and loses to O-LoRA on Order-4. The abstract's claim of 'significantly outperforms state-of-the-art' is not supported uniformly; for LLMs the text itself retreats to 'competitive.'

Total memory grows linearly with tasks (new ranks per task, frozen), and the pruning analysis only removes ~30% of parameters with visible accuracy drops (Last 80.9→79.5), weakening the efficiency story relative to methods with bounded footprints.

Key experimental details are under-specified or questionable: 'Fine-tune' Last (81.9) exceeds MoRAM on X-TAIL without clarification of the setting; significance testing covers only a subset of comparisons (Table 16); and the asymmetric parameterization (r*din trained keys but only k*dout trained values) is introduced without analysis of its consequences.

strengths: Broad and diverse empirical evaluation covering CLIP-based CL (X-TAIL, MTIL), LLM-based CL (TRACE, standard CL benchmarks, 15-task long sequences, SuperNI), and generalization after standard fine-tuning (CodeAlpaca/HumanEval with MMLU out-of-domain probes), which lends credibility to the central plasticity-stability claims.

The core design is simple and practical: decomposing rank-r LoRA updates into atomic rank-1 experts with frozen old atoms and incremental expansion, plus a router-free self-activation mechanism, yields strong results with very low per-task trainable parameter counts (4.4M, matching CoDyRA) and low GPU memory (Table 18).

Useful diagnostic analyses: ablations of routing strategies (Table 4), activation budget, temperature, and threshold (Fig. 4); per-token rank activation visualizations (Figs. 3, 6, 7) and aggregated activation statistics (Fig. 5) that qualitatively support claims of rank specialization, stable routing, and knowledge reuse; order-robustness analysis (Table 14); and post-pruning analysis (Tables 19, A.10).

The paper is generally well written, with a clear conceptual narrative (content-addressable retrieval vs. address-based routing), and hyperparameter details are provided in the appendix, which aids reproducibility.
An explicit impact statement discusses misuse and bias risks, which is appropriate.
weaknesses: The central narrative is partially contradicted by the paper's own ablations. In Table 4, Self-Activated Retrieval alone (60.26/65.94/69.85) underperforms the coarse MoE-LoRA baseline (62.56/69.45/74.53), and the bulk of the improvement comes from temperature scaling (79.62 Last) and the test-time threshold. The claim that the associative-memory/self-activation view is the key mechanism, rather than an aggressive sharpening heuristic, is therefore not well supported; the method reads more as a tuned sparse-gating pipeline than a validated replacement for routing.

The claimed three failure modes of coarse experts (interference, redundancy, routing collapse) are asserted rhetorically but not demonstrated with targeted evidence (e.g., no controlled measurement of router ambiguity growth, expert overlap, or interference as the expert pool expands). The Related Work and Method sections describe these phenomena as established facts without experiments backing them.

Novelty is incremental. Treating weight matrices as linear associative memories is a classical view (Kohonen 1972), and decomposing LoRA updates into rank-1 components with input-dependent mixtures is close to existing mixture-of-subspaces LoRA work (e.g., [87]); the router-free inner-product gating is a natural consequence rather than a substantially new mechanism. The paper should more sharply delineate what is new beyond assembling these ingredients.

Reported gains over strong baselines are often marginal: on TRACE the OP improvements over TreeLoRA are ~1 point (44.54 vs. 43.52 on LLaMA-2-7B); on SuperNI replay-based MoRAM is essentially tied with SAPT (51.79 vs. 51.54). The abstract's claim of 'significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines' is overstated for several benchmarks; the clearest wins are on X-TAIL Last/Average and SuperNI replay-free.

Internal inconsistencies in hyperparameters reduce confidence: Section 4.3 states a temperature of 0.01 was selected, while Appendix A.1 specifies 0.1 for CLIP X-TAIL and 0.5 for the CodeAlpaca experiment; temperatures vary widely across benchmarks, suggesting sensitivity and per-benchmark tuning that may not transfer. No code release is mentioned, further limiting reproducibility.

The self-activation score (Eq. 5) and its l2 normalization across the ensemble are ad hoc; no analysis of why this normalization is appropriate, how scores behave as r_t grows very large, or failure cases (e.g., degenerate keys, rank collapse) is provided.

Component ablation rows in Table 4 do not appear compositional (e.g., threshold-based selection alone gives 71.08 but 'Full' gives 80.90, versus 79.62 for temperature alone), and it is unclear how components interact; the ablation structure could be clarified.

Linear parameter growth per task persists despite pruning; the pruning experiment prunes ~30% of parameters while keeping 99% activation mass, but the effect on very long task streams (beyond 10-15 tasks) is not evaluated, so scalability claims about sub-linear expansion are not directly demonstrated.

Some presentation issues: Table 12's Transfer header block and per-dataset columns are dense and hard to parse; Fig. 2's panels are cluttered; the visualizations rely on a single layer (layer 8, K projection), which the appendix defends but which weakens generality of the qualitative claims.
